In the light of its golden wings.
 And when Sunset may breathe, from the lit Sea beneath,
40 Its ardours of rest and love,
And the crimson pall of eve may fall
From the depth of Heaven above,
With wings folded I rest, on mine aëry nest,
As still as a brooding dove.

paragraphs.source_en:
45 That orbèd maiden with white fire laden,
Whom mortals call the moon,
Glides glimmering o’er my fleecelike floor,
By the midnight breezes strewn;
And wherever the beat of her unseen feet,
50 Which only the angels hear,
May have broken the woof of my tent’s thin roof,
The stars peep behind her, and peer;
And I laugh to see them whirl and flee,
Like a swarm of golden bees,
55 When I widen the rent in my wind-built tent,

paragraphs.source_en:
breathe] The implicit analogy is between the sunset reflected from the sea and the perfume
exhaled by flowers: for similar synaesthesia cp. SP, Part First. ardours] glowing brilliancy, suggesting
intense desire: cp. WA 292, 340.
 love] Nbk 14; of love 1820, 1839. Chernaik (232) compares ‘of lawn and moss’ in the fair copy (Harvard
Nbk 1 p. 49) of SP 49 which becomes ‘of lawn and of moss’ in 1820.
 depth] depths Nbk 14.
 aëry] Nbk 14; airy 1820, 1839: both ‘elevated’ and ‘composed of air’.
 An echo of the apostrophe to the Holy Spirit in Paradise Lost i 19–21:
thou from the first
Wast present, and with mighty wings outspread
Dove-like satst brooding on the vast Abyss.
 white fire laden] See PU IV 219–23 and note.
 fleecelike] The comparison of cumulus clouds to fleece is a venerable commonplace: Aristophanes,
The Clouds 340–1; Lucretius, De Re. Nat. vi 504; L ii 25.
